questions.question: During branch-and-bound for an integer program, the term incumbent solution is used. Which solution is the incumbent at a given moment of the search?
options: The best integer-feasible solution found so far
The open node with the best LP relaxation value
The optimal solution of the integer program
The rounded optimum of the root LP relaxation

questions.question: In branch-and-bound, let $z_I$ be the objective value of the current incumbent and $z^*$ the optimal value of the integer program. Which bound does $z_I$ give?
options: $z^*\le z_I$ for maximization, $z^*\ge z_I$ for minimization
$z^*\ge z_I$ for maximization, $z^*\le z_I$ for minimization
$z^*=z_I$ for both maximization and minimization
$z^*\ge z_I$ for maximization and for minimization

questions.question: In branch-and-bound for a maximization integer program, a node's LP relaxation has a fractional optimal solution with value 25, higher than the current incumbent value 22. Why does this solution not become the incumbent?
options: Its point must first be rounded; the rounded point then takes over.
It is fractional, hence not feasible for the integer problem.
The incumbent may be replaced only by values from the root node.
Incumbents are replaced only after all open nodes are solved.

questions.question: A maximization integer program has only constraints $\sum_j a_{ij}x_j\le b_i$ with every $b_i\ge0$, and $x_j\ge0$ integer. Before any LP is solved, is an incumbent value available?
options: No: an incumbent exists only after the first LP is solved.
Yes: the all-zero point is feasible and is an incumbent.
No: the first incumbent must come from an integral node.
Yes: the root LP value can serve as the incumbent value.

questions.question: In branch-and-bound for a maximization integer program, there is no incumbent at first. The search then finds, in this order: an integer-feasible solution with value 9, a node with fractional LP optimum of value 14.2, and integer-feasible solutions with values 12 and 11. What is the incumbent value now?
options: 14.2, the best value seen so far
11, the latest feasible value found
12, the best feasible value found
9, the first feasible value found

questions.question: In branch-and-bound for a minimization integer program the incumbent costs 50. Next, a node gives an integral LP optimum costing 53, another node a fractional LP optimum costing 46, and a heuristic a verified feasible solution costing 48. What is the incumbent cost afterwards?
options: 46, from the fractional node
53, from the integral node
50, since heuristics do not count
48, from the heuristic solution

questions.question: For: maximize $3x_1+2x_2$ subject to $2x_1+3x_2\le12$, $4x_1+x_2\le10$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer, the LP relaxation optimum is $(1.8,2.8)$ with value 11. Which point can serve as an incumbent?
options: $(2,2)$, with value 10
$(2,3)$, with value 12
$(3,0)$, with value 9

questions.question: During branch-and-bound for a maximization integer program with optimal value $z^*$, the incumbent value is 13 and the largest LP bound among the open nodes is 15.5, with no other open nodes. Which statement about $z^*$ holds?
options: $z^*$ equals 13, the incumbent value
$z^*$ lies from 13 up to the bound 15.5
$z^*$ is at least 15.5, the open bound
$z^*$ is at most 13, the incumbent value

questions.question: A maximization mixed integer program requires $x$ to be an integer and lets $y\ge0$ be continuous. The incumbent value is 14. A node's LP relaxation has optimal solution $x=2$, $y=3.7$ with value 15. What happens to the incumbent?
options: It stays 14, as $y=3.7$ is fractional.
It becomes 15 only after $y$ is rounded to 4.
It becomes the point $(2,3.7)$ with value 15.
It stays 14 until the node is split on $y$.

questions.question: Branch-and-bound for a maximization integer program is stopped early because of a time limit. The incumbent has value 41 and the best open-node LP bound is 44.5 at a fractional point. Which decision should be implemented, and why?
options: The LP point, as its value 44.5 is the larger of the two values.
The LP point rounded, as it lies closest to the optimal value.
Neither, as no solution is valid before the search is finished.
The incumbent, as it is the only one meeting all restrictions.

questions.question: In branch-and-bound, a node has the original constraints plus branching constraints, and its LP relaxation optimum happens to be integral. Why is this point feasible for the original integer program, so that it can be an incumbent?
options: It meets only the branching constraints of its node.
It meets the original constraints, plus integrality.
Its value equals the LP bound of the root node.
It is optimal, and optimal points are always feasible.

questions.question: Branch-and-bound for a maximization integer program with optimal value $z^*$ has incumbent value 990, and the largest LP bound among the open nodes is 1000. Management accepts any plan whose value is at least 99% of $z^*$. May the search stop with the incumbent?
options: No: $10/990$ exceeds 1%, so the plan is too far off.
No: the search may stop only when the gap is zero.
Yes: $z^*=1000$, so the plan is exactly 1% below it.
Yes: 990 is at least 99% of any value $z^*\le1000$.

questions.question: For: maximize $5x_1+4x_2$ subject to $6x_1+4x_2\le24$, $x_1+2x_2\le6$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer, a heuristic gives the incumbent $(3,1)$ with value 19 before branching. The root is split on $x_2$; the child $x_2\ge2$ has LP value 18 and the child $x_2\le1$ has LP value $62/3$. Which child needs further work?
options: Both, as no node is closed before branching ends.
Only $x_2\ge2$, as its LP optimum is integral.
Only $x_2\le1$, since $62/3>19$ while $18<19$.
Neither, as the incumbent 19 is now proven optimal.

questions.question: In branch-and-bound for a maximization integer program the incumbent value is 17. A newly solved node has an integral LP optimum with value 16. A student replaces the incumbent, arguing that an integral LP optimum is optimal. What is wrong?
options: It is optimal only within its node, and 16 does not beat 17.
Nothing: an integral LP optimum always replaces the incumbent.
The point is infeasible, since node points are not original.
The node should be split first, to confirm integrality.

questions.question: Branch-and-bound for a maximization integer program has not yet found any feasible solution, so there is no incumbent. A node has LP bound 12, a fractional optimum and a feasible LP. Can this node be discarded because of its bound?
options: Yes: its bound 12 is below the root LP value, so it cannot be optimal.
Yes: a fractional optimum means the node contains no integer points.
No: without an incumbent there is nothing to compare the bound with.
No: nodes are never discarded until the first incumbent is optimal.

questions.question: In branch-and-bound for a maximization integer program whose objective has non-integer coefficients, after nodes 1 to 9 the incumbent values are none, 9, 9, 12, 13, 13, 13, 13, 13 and the best remaining bounds are 16, 16, 15.5, 15.5, 14.5, 14.5, 13.8, 13.4, 13. When was an optimal solution first held, and when was it proven optimal?
options: Held after node 5, proven after node 9
Held after node 9, proven after node 9
Held after node 2, proven after node 5
Held after node 5, proven after node 5

questions.question: For: maximize $5x_1+4x_2$ subject to $6x_1+4x_2\le24$, $x_1+2x_2\le6$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer, the incumbent is $(2,2)$ with value 18 and the only open node, $x_2\le1$, has LP value $62/3\approx20.67$. A student then checks that $(4,0)$ is feasible. What follows?
options: $(4,0)$ is incumbent, but the open node may beat 20.
$(2,2)$ stays, as $(4,0)$ was not found by branching.
$20.67$ becomes the incumbent value, the open node's bound.
$(4,0)$, value 20, is incumbent and is proven optimal.
